composition: Nominal composition (wt.%) of alloy S1: 0.98 C, 6.00 Al, 0.99 Mn, 0.33 Si, 0.49 Mo, 0.0036 B, balance Fe; Ni and Ti were not added. The design is that of a low-density nano-bainitic steel: Al at 5.8–8 wt.% lowers density (about 1.3 % per 1 wt.% Al), stabilizes ferrite, accelerates the bainitic transformation and refines the bainitic lamellae, while Mn is limited to ~1 wt.% and high C (0.9–1.0 wt.%) is required to achieve full austenitization without polygonal ferrite (αp) and to hold Ms near 300 °C. Si is kept low (0.33 wt.%) because Al also suppresses carbide precipitation, Mo is added for hardenability, and B microalloying (0.0036 wt.%) further improves hardenability without harming the bainitic transformation.
conclusions: Within the ≥6 wt.% Al group, S1 austempered at 350 °C shows the fastest bainitic transformation (Bt ≈ 1600 s, incubation 100 s) and belongs, with S2, to the intermediate-fast range (Bt 1600–4000 s) of the study; its TA 1150 °C / TB 350 °C condition gives ~1380 MPa UTS, 8.7 % El, 464 HV30 and PSE ≈ 12,000 MPa·%. S1 and S2 differ by only ~0.1 wt.% C and show a minor mechanical difference, since ~1 wt.% C variations are secondary to the Al level in setting the strength–ductility balance. Its strength–ductility product is somewhat below that of the Ti-microalloyed S4 (PSE ≈ 13,600 MPa·%; best average/maximum elongation of the study) but clearly above the high-Al S3, which loses ductility at low austempering temperature (El ≈ 2.4 %, PSE ≈ 3480 MPa·%). Overall the work shows that alloy composition and microstructural features (lath thickness and its spread, retained-austenite fraction and stability) govern the bainitic transformation and the resulting strength–ductility response of low-density Al–C nano-bainitic steels, with TB acting as the principal lever on the UTS–El trade-off.
mechanisms: Austenitizing at 1150 °C for 15 min dissolves carbides and suppresses polygonal ferrite (the S1 matrix is αp-free at 1150 °C although αp persists at the 1050 °C benchmark), yielding a chemically homogeneous austenite; fixing TA at 1150 °C for S1, S2, S4 and S5 makes the observed differences in bainitic transformation attributable to composition and TB rather than to prior austenite condition.

Cooling at 100 K s⁻¹ is fast enough to suppress intermediate phase transformations and ensure a fine bainitic transformation, but (Fe,M)xCy nucleates during this cooling stage because of its extremely high nucleation kinetics between ~700 and 1150 °C, so its avoidance is practically impossible and primary precipitation occurs above the austempering temperature.

Austempering at 350 °C, just above the measured Ms of 277 °C, drives the displacive growth of nano-scale bainitic ferrite laths (nB Type 1 and Type 2); the transformation finishes in ~1600 s after an incubation time of ~100 s, the fastest among the ≥6 wt.% Al steels.

A higher austempering temperature (350 °C vs 300 °C) coarsens the bainitic laths (mean Lt(t) 55 nm vs 35 nm) and broadens the thickness distribution (SD 23 nm vs 11 nm), which lowers UTS while raising elongation.

The high C–Al alloy concept produces an incomplete bainitic reaction: as bainite forms, the untransformed austenite becomes C-enriched and chemically stabilized, so Vγ rises to 34 % at 350 °C (versus 27 % at 300 °C).

The large retained-austenite fraction (34 %) supplies TRIP-assisted strain hardening, which improves total elongation to 8.7 % at the expense of strength (~1380 MPa UTS) relative to the 300 °C condition.

The (Fe,M)xCy carbides are cementite-like and modified by entrapped Si (rapid cooling prevents the equilibrium exclusion of Si from Fe3C) and by Mo, which stabilizes them; their accelerated nucleation and rounded, spherical morphology mean no micro-voids form at these particles, so they have a negligible influence on tensile properties.

The broad Lt(t) distribution at 350 °C reflects the coexistence of nB Type 1 and Type 2 with blocky retained austenite between them, producing an interlocked bainitic morphology; this heterogeneity of lath thickness is strongest in the higher-alloyed S1–S3 steels and is considered an elongation-improving factor relative to lower-alloying concepts.

The higher εα micro-strain (0.45 % vs 0.35 % in γr) at 350 °C indicates a more heterogeneous dislocation distribution in bainitic ferrite, consistent with the strain partitioning between the bainitic ferrite and retained austenite that controls the strength–ductility trade-off.
microstructure: After austenitizing at 1150 °C the matrix is free of polygonal ferrite (αp-free according to LOM with 6 % Nital etching); the same steel still shows αp at the 1050 °C benchmark, so 1150 °C is the temperature at which carbide dissolution is advanced, homogenization improved and αp suppressed. Austempering at 350 °C produces a nano-bainitic (nB) structure built from nano-scale bainitic ferrite (αb, bcc) laths/needles of nB Type 1 and Type 2, inter- and intra-sheaf blocky retained austenite (γr, fcc), and cementite-like (Fe,M)xCy (M = Si, Mo) precipitates. Three phases were identified. The mean true lamellar thickness Lt(t) of bainitic ferrite is 55 nm with a standard deviation of 23 nm, the broad thickness range reflecting the coexistence of the two nB types together with blocky γr between them (an interlocked bainitic morphology). Retained austenite reaches 34 vol.% — a pronounced incomplete-reaction structure. XRD Rietveld analysis gives micro-strains of εγ = 0.35 % for retained austenite and εα = 0.45 % for bainitic ferrite; the notably higher εα at 350 °C indicates a clearer heterogeneous dislocation distribution. (Fe,M)xCy precipitates are rounded/equiaxed and located near the γr–bainitic ferrite phase boundaries; they formed primarily during cooling/prior processing above the bainitic hold temperature and produced no observable micro-voids. The αb/γr interface is the principal phase boundary considered; no explicit interfacial coherency data are reported for S1. Phase evolution follows austenitization (carbide dissolution, αp elimination) → cooling at 100 K s⁻¹ with (Fe,M)xCy nucleation above the hold temperature → growth of bainitic ferrite laths with blocky retained austenite between sheaves during the 350 °C hold.
processing: Steel blocks were cast in a vacuum arc furnace, homogenized at 1100 °C for 24 h under inert argon protection to promote uniform composition and microstructure, then step-by-step hot rolled to a thickness of ~11 mm and slow cooled in the oven. Samples were precisely fabricated by water-jet cutting (OMAX 2626, Kent, Washington, USA) to minimize thermal distortion, and cylindrical dilatometer specimens (∅5 × 10 mm³) plus ASTM E8 sub-size tensile specimens were heat-treated in a DIL 805A dilatometer (TA Instruments). The thermal cycle (Fig. 1a) comprised heating at 10 K s⁻¹ to the austenitizing temperature of 1150 °C with a 15 min hold, continuous cooling at 100 K s⁻¹ to the austempering temperature (fast enough to suppress intermediate phase transformations and ensure a fine bainitic transformation), an isothermal bainitic hold at TB = 350 °C for the transformation finish time Bt ≈ 1600 s, and a final cooling. The austempering temperature was deliberately chosen just above the measured Ms of 277 °C to obtain a nano-bainitic microstructure. This heat-treatment lineage sits downstream of the shared casting/homogenization/hot-rolling route applied to all steels of the study, with a fixed TA = 1150 °C used for S1, S2, S4 and S5 so that differences in transformation behaviour reflect composition and TB rather than prior austenite condition.
properties: Tensile specimens (ASTM E8 sub-size round: 12.5 mm gauge length, 2.5 mm diameter, 7 mm shoulder length), heat-treated in the DIL 805A dilatometer with the Fig. 1(a) cycle and tested on a Zwick/Roell universal testing machine (250 kN load cell), give an ultimate tensile strength of ~1380 MPa and a total elongation of 8.7 % for this TA 1150 °C / TB 350 °C condition. Bulk hardness is 464 HV30, and the product of strength and elongation (PSE) is ~12,000 MPa·%. For comparison, the same alloy austempered at the lower TB of 300 °C reaches ~1600 MPa UTS and ~497 HV30 at only 6.8 % El (PSE ≈ 10,880 MPa·%). The strongest strength–ductility balance among the studied steels is obtained by the Ti-microalloyed S4 (PSE ≈ 13,600 MPa·% at TA 1150 °C, TB 320 °C), i.e. slightly superior to S1 despite S4's lower carbon content. Characterization techniques applied to this sample and its condition include dilatometry (RLC vs time/temperature and Ms tangent-intersection analysis), light optical microscopy (6 % Nital), X-ray diffraction with Rietveld refinement of Vγ and micro-strain (the S1 XRD pattern is the article's worked example for Vγ determination), SEM/EDX for lath thickness and (Fe,M)xCy precipitate analysis, EBSD, and MatCalc equilibrium/precipitation-kinetics simulations. Physical, chemical and radiation-related properties were not measured.
summary: S1 is a low-density, high C–Al nano-bainitic (nB) steel (0.98 wt.% C, 6.00 wt.% Al) fabricated by vacuum arc casting, homogenization, hot rolling and water-jet cutting, then heat-treated in a DIL 805A dilatometer: austenitized at TA = 1150 °C for 15 min, cooled at 100 K s⁻¹ and austempered at TB = 350 °C, i.e. just above its measured Ms of 277 °C, until the bainitic transformation finished in ~1600 s. The sample addresses how C–Al alloying and austempering temperature govern bainitic transformation kinetics, the resulting nano-scale bainitic ferrite + retained austenite microstructure, and the strength–ductility balance of low-density steels.
unmapped: Dilatometry/MatCalc framework for S1: measured Ms = 277 °C (tangent-intersection of the cooling RLC–T curve), MatCalc ferrite-free TA = 991 °C and operational (derivative-based) measured TA = 1062 °C, with carbide-dissolution temperature Tcd ≈ 1103 °C; the applied TA was set at 1150 °C.

The S1 steel's MatCalc equilibrium phase-fraction diagram (Fig. 2b) gives a grey band covering TB 300–350 °C and a matrix fraction (1 − Vc) = 0.78, used to correct the XRD-based Vγ calculation; the S1 XRD pattern is the article's illustrative example (Fig. 2a) with the (111)γ, (110)α, (200)γ, (200)α, (220)γ, (211)α, (311)γ and (220)α reflections.

The TTP diagram of S1 (TA 1150 °C, cooling rate 100 K s⁻¹) shows a (Fe,M)xCy C-shaped nose near 900–1000 °C at ~10⁻³–10⁻² s with 5/50/95 % transformation curves and TB lines at 350 °C (Bt 2300 s) and 300 °C (Bt 3600 s); this panel is also taken to approximately represent S2.

EDX of the (Fe,M)xCy particles in S1 (Fig. 9, Spec.1/Spec.2) confirmed a cementite-like composition modified by Si and Mo; carbon could not be quantified reliably by EDX, so it was used only to identify the carbides.

Insoluble/unresolved: no unambiguous κ-carbide was observed microscopically; because Mn is limited to ~1 wt.%, κ-carbides are presumed to persist only as nanoscale, embedded, non-stoichiometric L1₂-type structures in the matrix.
